stories.headline: Update: Trump Says Iran Decision Coming 'Very Soon' as U.S. Weighs Military and Diplomatic Options
stories.summary:
President Trump told reporters Thursday that a decision on Iran is coming "very soon," as the administration continues to assess possible responses following the collapse of nuclear talks and the expulsion of the Iranian diplomatic delegation from the United States. The remarks come amid heightened U.S.-Iran tensions spanning multiple fronts, including the Fairford terror plot, ongoing proxy conflicts, and intensifying economic pressure campaigns.

Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent this week warned that Iran could have "nothing left to trade" within two weeks under current sanctions pressure. Iranian Parliament Speaker Mohammad Bagher Ghalibaf pushed back sharply on Thursday, rejecting Bessent's collapse narrative and using social media memes to argue that the United States itself faces a debt crisis, citing rising Treasury yields and energy costs.

The standoff is being tracked across more than 20 news outlets, reflecting its broad significance. Supporters of the administration's approach argue maximum economic pressure is the surest path to a deal or regime capitulation; critics warn that the rhetoric raises the risk of military miscalculation with a nuclear-threshold state. The story is fast-moving, with Trump's promised decision potentially arriving within days.

stories.headline: FBI Arrests Energy Department Employee at Nuclear Site on Charges of Aiding Houthis
stories.summary:
The FBI arrested a Department of Energy employee Thursday at the Hanford nuclear site in Washington state on charges of attempting to provide material support to the Houthis, the Iranian-backed militant group designated as a foreign terrorist organization. The suspect, Ashton Hamed Ellaboudy, 51, of Richland, Washington, is accused of acquiring materials for homemade explosives and drones with the intent of aiding the group.

According to the Justice Department, Ellaboudy also allegedly contacted Katie Miller, wife of White House Deputy Chief of Staff Stephen Miller, more than 40 times over less than two months. The nature and content of those contacts were not immediately detailed in public charging documents.

The arrest is notable both for the suspect's position at a sensitive federal nuclear facility and for the alleged connection to the Houthis, who have been at the center of ongoing U.S. military operations in the Red Sea region. The case is being prosecuted federally under material support statutes that carry severe penalties. The DOE said it is cooperating fully with the Justice Department's investigation.

stories.headline: NASA Launches Crew-13 to International Space Station; Jessica Watkins Becomes First Black Woman to Lead Crew to Orbit
stories.summary:
Four astronauts lifted off Thursday from Cape Canaveral Space Force Station aboard a SpaceX Dragon capsule, bound for the International Space Station on a mission scheduled to last until spring 2027. The crew is commanded by NASA astronaut Jessica Watkins, who became the first Black woman to lead a crew to orbit. The launch had been delayed three weeks to repair a fuel system leak in the Dragon capsule.

The crew includes NASA astronaut Luke Delaney, a retired Marine; Canadian Space Agency astronaut Joshua Kutryk, a Royal Canadian Air Force colonel whose wife is due to give birth in late November while he is aboard the station; and Russian cosmonaut Sergey Teteryatnikov, a former submariner. They will relieve four astronauts who have been living at the orbiting laboratory since February.

This marked SpaceX's 13th operational crew mission for NASA. The transit to the station was expected to take approximately eight hours, one of the fastest crew transits yet attempted. The mission comes as the International Space Station approaches a planned decommissioning in the late 2020s, making long-duration science and operations missions like Crew-13 increasingly important for research continuity.

stories.headline: Update: Tennessee Execution Attempt Fails After Supreme Court Vacates Stay, Then Lethal Injection Is Halted
stories.summary:
Convicted killer Christa Pike, 50, was set to become the first woman executed in Tennessee since the early 1800s, but Wednesday's execution attempt failed after complications during the lethal injection process. The U.S. Supreme Court had vacated a stay issued by the Sixth Circuit Court of Appeals, clearing the way for the execution to proceed, but the procedure was ultimately halted before Pike was pronounced dead.

Pike was convicted of the 1995 murder of 19-year-old Colleen Slemmer in Knoxville, a killing prosecutors described as a brutal, prolonged attack carried out with a box cutter and meat cleaver. She was 18 at the time of the crime. The Supreme Court's decision to lift the Sixth Circuit stay was 6-3, with Justices Sotomayor, Kagan, and Brown Jackson dissenting, arguing the lower court should have been given time to weigh Pike's pending legal challenge before irreversible action was taken.

The failed execution raises immediate questions about Tennessee's lethal injection protocol and what comes next legally for Pike. Executions that are halted due to procedural failure have historically prompted legal challenges over whether a second attempt constitutes cruel and unusual punishment under the Eighth Amendment.

The case draws national attention as one of the rare instances of a woman facing execution in the modern era and as an example of the ongoing legal battles over capital punishment procedures. Supporters of the execution argued Pike's crime was premeditated and heinous; opponents, including the dissenting justices, contended the legal process was rushed.

stories.headline: Trump Administration Issues $500 ACA Refund Checks to Nearly 1 Million Americans
stories.summary:
The Trump administration has begun distributing $500 refund checks to approximately 950,000 Americans in 30 states who purchased health insurance through the federal HealthCare.gov exchange without receiving government subsidies. Each check is accompanied by a personal letter from President Trump asserting that the Biden administration had allowed a surplus to accumulate from a 'user fee' charged to operate the federal exchange, and that those funds rightfully belong to consumers.

The 30 states involved are those that do not operate their own Affordable Care Act exchanges and instead rely on the federal government's platform, which charges insurers a fee for services. The administration says it has also significantly reduced those fees going forward. Texas leads all states with an estimated 139,000 recipients, followed by Florida with 127,900 and Ohio with 65,700.

The White House has framed the move as correcting what it calls overcharging under the previous administration and as part of a broader effort to reform and reduce the scope of the ACA. Critics and Democrats are likely to contest the characterization that the surplus represents consumer overcharges, arguing the fees fund legitimate exchange operations and that the disbursement is a political maneuver ahead of the midterm elections.

The action affects roughly 1 million households across the country and represents a significant executive-branch intervention in the health insurance market. It comes as the administration has separately moved to remove millions from ACA rolls it characterizes as fraudulent enrollees.

stories.headline: Family of Renee Good, Killed by ICE Agent in Minneapolis, Files Federal Wrongful Death Lawsuit
stories.summary:
The family of Renee Good, a 37-year-old woman fatally shot by a federal immigration officer in Minneapolis on January 7, filed two federal lawsuits Thursday alleging wrongful death, civil rights violations, and a government conspiracy to conceal evidence. The suits were brought by Good's partner, Becca Good, and her brother, Brent Ganger, and name the U.S. government and several immigration officials as defendants.

Good was killed during a wave of immigration enforcement operations in Minneapolis. Bystander video shows her sitting in a car blocking a road while honking her horn during an immigration operation in her neighborhood. Federal officers ordered her to exit the vehicle; when the car began to move, an officer fired into the windshield and then twice more through the driver's window, fatally wounding her. Federal officials initially said the officer acted in self-defense and described Good's actions as 'an act of domestic terrorism.'

The wrongful death lawsuit seeks damages for Good's death and the suffering of her family. A separate suit alleges a conspiracy to interfere with civil rights and seeks a jury trial, claiming the government moved to suppress evidence of what occurred. Minnesota state prosecutors have separately been investigating the shootings and have sought evidence withheld by federal authorities.

The case has become a flashpoint in the national debate over immigration enforcement tactics. Supporters of the administration's enforcement posture argue officers acted lawfully in a dangerous situation; critics and civil liberties advocates contend the shooting illustrates a pattern of excessive force during immigration raids and a lack of federal accountability.

stories.headline: Former Dallas Officer Amber Guyger, Convicted of Murdering Botham Jean in His Own Apartment, Granted Parole
stories.summary:
The Texas Board of Pardons and Parole on Thursday approved parole for Amber Guyger, the former Dallas police officer convicted of murder in the 2018 killing of Botham Jean. Guyger, 38, will be released after serving seven years of a 10-year sentence. The board rejected her initial parole application in 2024 but approved her release over the objections of Jean's family on her next eligible application.

Guyger, who was white, shot Jean, a 26-year-old Black accountant from St. Lucia, after entering his fourth-floor apartment while still in uniform following a long shift. She testified she believed she had entered her own apartment one floor below and mistook Jean for an intruder. The shooting drew intense national attention as one in a series of killings of Black men by white police officers and became a reference point in debates over police use of force and accountability.

Jean's family strongly opposed the parole. Civil rights attorney Lee Merritt, representing the family, said: 'A 10-year sentence was already a fraction of what was lost. Releasing Ms. Guyger after seven years makes that loss feel even smaller in the eyes of the system.' In 2024, a federal civil jury ordered Guyger to pay Jean's family nearly $100 million in damages.

The board said its decision was based on a review of extensive records, noting Guyger had no documented pattern of violent or assaultive behavior and had completed required prison programs. The Texas Department of Criminal Justice will determine the specific release date. The case continues to carry national significance in ongoing debates about racial justice and police accountability.

stories.headline: Update: Putin Threatens Nuclear Use Over Kaliningrad as Russia-NATO Tensions Escalate
stories.summary:
Russian President Vladimir Putin warned Thursday that Russia would deploy all weapons at its disposal, including nuclear arms, if it faced a direct attack on its Baltic exclave of Kaliningrad. Speaking at the Valdai foreign policy forum, Putin said the threat was a response to Western statements that Moscow was preparing for war in 2029 or 2030, insisting Russia was 'not threatening anyone' but merely reacting to NATO posturing.

Throughout the week, Russia has accused NATO of planning to blockade Kaliningrad, which borders NATO members Lithuania and Poland. NATO has sought to de-escalate the situation, calling itself a defensive alliance and urging Moscow to halt its nuclear rhetoric. German Chancellor Friedrich Merz said Thursday that Germany was preparing for further Russian hybrid attacks, including 'serious ones,' citing a drone found at Leipzig airport near Ukrainian cargo planes in August.

Putin also addressed the war in Ukraine, again blaming the West for provoking Russia's 2022 invasion and saying Russia's attacks on Ukrainian energy infrastructure were retaliatory. He acknowledged Ukraine's drone strikes on Russian oil refineries had cost Russia about 1% of GDP. A key bridge in Kyiv was struck by Russian drones on Thursday, continuing a pattern of attacks on civilian infrastructure.

The Kaliningrad threats represent a significant new escalation in Putin's public nuclear signaling, arriving as the Russia-Iran war against the West continues to reshape global security and energy markets. Western officials have repeatedly characterized such nuclear warnings as coercive rhetoric rather than concrete military intent, but the statements have heightened alarm among Baltic NATO members who share borders with the Russian exclave.

stories.headline: Update: New Arrest in RAF Fairford Terror Plot as Iran Denies Involvement
stories.summary:
British counterterrorism police arrested a 27-year-old dual U.K.-Iranian national Thursday on suspicion of plotting a terrorist attack, the latest development in an ongoing investigation linked to a security incident near RAF Fairford in Gloucestershire. Officers simultaneously searched two properties in London. RAF Fairford, located roughly 100 miles west of London, has served as a staging base for American bombers during the ongoing U.S.-Iran conflict.

Five British men in their 20s were arrested Sunday near the base on suspicion of explosives and terrorism offenses; gasoline was found in three vans connected to them, though no explosives were recovered. All five have since been released on bail, a decision publicly criticized by both President Trump and Secretary of State Marco Rubio. A sixth individual was interviewed under caution but not arrested.

British Prime Minister Andy Burnham has said there are 'strong indications' Iran was involved in the plot, while Tehran has denied any role. The senior national counterterrorism coordinator said investigators are examining 'all possible angles — including possible foreign state involvement.' The incident is being treated as one of the most serious suspected state-sponsored terrorism plots on U.K. soil in recent years.

Thursday's arrest adds a new suspect to the investigation and intensifies pressure on the British government to respond more forcefully. The episode comes amid broader concerns about Iranian hybrid operations targeting Western countries supporting the U.S. in the ongoing conflict, following the earlier confirmed Iranian link to a foiled attack also involving the Fairford base.

stories.headline: Update: French Student Protests Turn Violent; 625 Arrested, Schools Blocked Nationwide
stories.summary:
French student protests escalated sharply Thursday, with Prime Minister Sébastien Lecornu convening an emergency crisis meeting and canceling ministerial travel as unrest spread across the Paris region and to cities including Lyon, Marseille, Rouen, and others. More than 625 people, mostly students, have been arrested over two days of demonstrations. Over 350 high schools and roughly 30 university campuses were affected Thursday alone, with police deploying tear gas in multiple locations.

The protests, which began last week, center on student grievances including teacher shortages, dilapidated school buildings, overcrowded classrooms, and long schedules. They have intensified following the government's announcement of a series of spending cuts in its 2027 budget. Eighty-three police and gendarmes were wounded Thursday; 119 students and school staff have been injured since the unrest began. In Marseille, the principal of a high school was doused in gasoline and injured, while two other principals were attacked in Rouen and Petit-Quevilly.

Interior Minister Laurent Nunez warned that outside agitators had moved between schools to incite students to violence. Education Minister Edouard Geffray called on schools to shift to remote learning if protests blocked access, saying 'violence will not keep our students from their fundamental right to an education.' The government faces pressure from both the left, which sympathizes with students' material grievances, and the right, which has condemned the destruction and called for firmer police action.

The crisis represents a significant political challenge for the Lecornu government at a sensitive budgetary moment. Analysts note that while student complaints about school conditions are widely acknowledged as legitimate, the turn toward arson, assaults on administrators, and attacks on firefighters has alienated some public sympathy and given the government grounds to frame the unrest as driven by extremist elements rather than genuine reform demands.

stories.headline: 10-Year Treasury Yields Hit 24-Year High, Pushing Mortgage Rates Higher
stories.summary:
The yield on the 10-year U.S. Treasury bond topped 5.34 percent on Thursday, its highest level since April 2002, as investors continued to grapple with persistent inflation and elevated government debt levels. The surge in yields signals expectations of higher borrowing costs across the economy for the foreseeable future, with analysts noting that the ongoing U.S. war with Iran and structural fiscal pressures are key drivers unlikely to ease soon.

The rise in Treasury yields is already feeding into consumer borrowing costs. The average 30-year fixed-rate mortgage has climbed to 7.28 percent, up from 6.34 percent a year ago, pushing more homebuyers toward adjustable-rate mortgages as affordability deteriorates. Higher yields also increase the cost of government debt service, intensifying pressure on federal finances.

The development comes amid broader midterm-season economic anxiety, with wages lagging inflation and household pocketbook stress weighing on voter sentiment. Analysts say the combination of geopolitical risk premiums from the Iran conflict and high domestic debt levels creates a difficult environment for the Federal Reserve as it weighs its next policy moves.

Market observers note that a sustained break above 5.34 percent on the 10-year could further tighten financial conditions across mortgages, auto loans, corporate credit, and government borrowing — amplifying economic headwinds heading into the final stretch before November's midterm elections.

stories.headline: Update: Netanyahu Says Flydubai Attacker Underwent Islamist Radicalization; UAE Investigates Terrorism Link
stories.summary:
Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu said Thursday that investigations indicate the man who stabbed a pilot and attempted to crash a Dubai-to-Tel Aviv Flydubai flight had undergone "Islamist radical indoctrination." Speaking to Fox News, Netanyahu described the attacker — identified as an Omani national — as suicidal, noting he shouted "kill me, kill me" after being subdued by passengers and crew. Netanyahu said it appeared "very likely" the attacker intended to bring down the plane but stopped short of drawing final conclusions.

The UAE's state news agency confirmed Thursday that investigations have been launched to determine whether the incident was linked to terrorist activity. The co-pilot who carried out the attack is currently being held in Saudi Arabia, where the aircraft made an emergency landing after a controlled 17,000-foot plunge in altitude, but UAE officials assert jurisdictional authority because the aircraft is UAE-registered. Netanyahu said the attacker is expected to be transferred to the UAE.

Israeli intelligence agency Mossad has been conducting its own investigation, interviewing passengers after they arrived in Tel Aviv. Preliminary findings from that probe, shared with BBC Arabic, concluded the attacker intended to crash the plane. Both Netanyahu and Indian Prime Minister Narendra Modi praised the stabbed pilot, Indian national Captain Smit Machchhar, as a hero; India's ambassador to the UAE visited him in hospital Thursday.

The incident — involving more than 170 passengers — has drawn attention from multiple governments and intelligence agencies. When asked whether Iran was involved, Netanyahu said it was "too early to say." The episode adds to regional security tensions at a time of ongoing U.S.-Iran conflict.

stories.headline: Russia Warned Garry Kasparov His Life Is in Danger, U.S. and Lithuanian Security Services Say
stories.summary:
Exiled Russian chess legend and opposition activist Garry Kasparov says he was warned by American and Lithuanian security services that his life is in danger, in connection with an alleged Kremlin-linked assassination network. Kasparov, who lives in the United States, wrote in his publication The Next Move that he and fellow Free Russia Forum co-founder Ivan Tyutrin had been advised to take precautions, though he said he had not been told explicitly he was a confirmed target.

The warning is linked to a U.S. Justice Department indictment unsealed earlier this month charging five individuals alleged to be part of a Kremlin-directed network — dubbed the RIS Network — plotting attacks and murders against Russian dissidents and defectors in multiple countries, including the United States. Spanish newspaper El Mundo reported that Kasparov was placed under enhanced protection over the summer for the first time since relocating to the U.S. All five alleged organizers remain at large.

Kasparov, who retired from competitive chess in 2005 to oppose Putin before fleeing Russia in 2013, said he would not stop his activism despite the threat. "My family and I will not truly be safe as long as Putin is in power in Russia," he wrote. Russia has classified him as a foreign agent and listed him as a terrorist and extremist — designations he rejects.

The Kremlin has not directly addressed the specific allegations against Kasparov. The alleged network is said to have been operating since at least 2024, and U.S. officials have described it as a "global assassination network" that attempted to recruit U.S. citizens to carry out killings. The case marks a new and direct intersection of Russian state violence and U.S. domestic security.

stories.headline: Update: Drone Strikes Hit Ethiopian Capital as Civil War Escalates
stories.summary:
Explosions were heard overnight in Addis Ababa, Ethiopia's capital, with residents and diplomatic sources reporting blasts near the military headquarters in the west and near a secret service base in the south. The blasts came hours after the government banned drone flights over the city, and a source linked to opposition fighters told Reuters that rebel forces were responsible for what they described as drone strikes.

The attacks follow a week of escalating fighting between the Ethiopian army and a newly formed alliance of armed groups, including forces from the Tigray region and the Amhara militia known as Fano. The alliance, formed last month, has stated its goal is the removal of Prime Minister Abiy Ahmed's government. The national army and a pro-government militia are reported to be advancing toward Mekelle, Tigray's main city, while the TPLF is also fighting in the strategic Afar region.

Eritrea has denied allegations from Addis Ababa that it is backing the rebel alliance. Internet and telecoms access in Tigray have been cut, making independent verification of ground conditions difficult. A medic in the southern Tigrayan town of Alamata reported 52 civilian deaths in three days of fighting earlier this week. The renewed conflict risks reigniting a civil war that, by one African Union estimate, cost 600,000 lives between 2020 and 2022.

stories.headline: Pakistani Airstrikes Kill 10 Civilians, Mostly Children, in Afghanistan, UN Says
stories.summary:
Pakistan launched airstrikes overnight in Afghanistan's Kunar and Helmand provinces, killing at least 10 civilians — most of them children — and wounding nine others, according to the United Nations Mission in Afghanistan (UNAMA). Afghanistan's Taliban government condemned the strikes as an act of aggression, saying three civilian homes were destroyed and that women and children were among the dead.

Pakistan's Ministry of Information offered a sharply different account, stating the strikes were "intelligence-driven, well planned and calibrated" operations targeting militant hideouts linked to Pakistani insurgent groups responsible for cross-border attacks. The ministry claimed 22 "terrorists" were killed and large quantities of weapons destroyed, and vowed that operations would "continue at full pace."

One resident in Kunar province told CBS News that a strike hit a home belonging to a family that had moved in only one day earlier, killing all six members including children. Cross-border clashes between Pakistan and Afghanistan have escalated significantly in 2026, with UNAMA reporting more than 1,100 civilian deaths and injuries in Afghanistan from such incidents this year alone. The strikes add pressure to an already volatile relationship between Islamabad and the Taliban government in Kabul.

stories.headline: Musk Named Co-Lead of Pentagon's Project Meridian on Future Warfare
stories.summary:
Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth announced Wednesday that Elon Musk will co-lead Project Meridian, a new Pentagon initiative tasked with mapping emerging domains of warfare and identifying weapons and technology the U.S. military will need to dominate them in the coming decades. Musk will work alongside defense tech billionaire Palmer Luckey, founder of Anduril Industries, and former House Speaker Newt Gingrich, under the direction of Pentagon Chief Technology Officer Emil Michael.

Hegseth framed the initiative as a recognition that the "best forecasters of future conflict do not solely reside inside the Pentagon," arguing that outside expertise is needed to avoid institutional bias. Project Meridian has a 120-day mandate to produce a public report and a classified annex on future warfare domains, spanning what Hegseth described as a scope "from under the Earth to beyond the moon."

The appointment raises potential conflict-of-interest questions: Musk's SpaceX is a major Pentagon contractor, and Luckey's Anduril specializes in autonomous weapons systems that compete for the same defense contracts the project may ultimately shape. Critics are likely to scrutinize whether executives whose companies stand to benefit financially should be directing the military's long-range technology planning. Supporters argue their hands-on experience with cutting-edge defense technology makes them uniquely qualified for the task.

stories.headline: Update: Rubio Expels Iranian Delegation from U.S. as Nuclear Talks Collapse
stories.summary:
Secretary of State Marco Rubio ordered the Iranian delegation attending the United Nations General Assembly to immediately leave the United States after peace negotiations between Washington and Tehran broke down, according to a U.S. official and a second source with knowledge of the matter. Rubio determined the Iranians had "overstayed their welcome" following the failure of Qatari-mediated talks aimed at ending the nearly nine-month U.S.-Iran conflict.

The move is described as a highly unusual diplomatic rebuke, even accounting for the fact that the Iranian delegation was likely to depart the country soon regardless. The expulsion lays bare the deep distrust between the two governments and signals a significant hardening of the U.S. posture following the collapse of ceasefire negotiations. Iranian state media separately reported that Tehran had received a formal U.S. counterproposal to its seven-day ceasefire plan, which the White House had previously rejected.

The diplomatic rupture comes as Iranian President Masoud Pezeshkian accused the United States and Israel of trying to foment internal divisions in Iran, and as the Iranian rial hit record lows amid ongoing conflict pressure. The situation marks a concrete deterioration from earlier mediation efforts and raises fresh concern among officials who have warned that military conflict is growing more likely.

stories.headline: Senate Confirms Keith Sonderling as Labor Secretary; Democrats Block Data Center Bill
stories.summary:
The Senate voted 47-41 along party lines Wednesday to confirm Keith Sonderling as Secretary of Labor, filling a cabinet seat that had been officially vacant since April when Lori Chavez-DeRemer departed. Sonderling had been serving in an acting capacity and his confirmation required only a simple majority under current Senate rules. All Republicans present voted for confirmation; all Democrats voted against.

Separately, Senate Democrats blocked the Ratepayer Protection Act, a bill aimed at preventing data centers from driving up local electricity costs for consumers. The legislation had passed the House 417-3 with overwhelming bipartisan support. Republicans accused Democrats of playing election-year politics, while Democrats argued the bill was "toothless" and lacked meaningful limits on AI use or deployment.

The twin votes illustrate the sharply partisan dynamics in the Senate five weeks before midterm elections. Democrats also blocked a Republican measure that would have restricted congressional stock trading, objecting to an attached voter ID provision that Minority Leader Chuck Schumer called "trickery." Republicans countered that Democrats were denying voters progress on issues — stock trading and energy costs — that have broad public support.

stories.headline: Newsom Signs AI Worker Protection Laws, Criticizes Trump's Self-Regulation Approach
stories.summary:
California Gov. Gavin Newsom signed a package of laws Wednesday aimed at protecting workers from artificial intelligence risks, including bans on employers using AI to predict workers' emotional states via biometric data, requirements that employers notify workers in writing if AI triggers mass layoffs, and prohibitions on using AI as the sole basis for firing an employee. Newsom also signed an executive order directing state agencies to continue using the term "artificial intelligence" rather than "super intelligence," the term President Trump recently ordered U.S. diplomats to adopt.

The signing came one day after Trump convened top technology executives at the White House to sign a voluntary self-regulation accord on AI safety, which Newsom sharply criticized. "We have to do a lot more in the absence of federal leadership," Newsom said, leaving open the possibility of calling a special legislative session on AI oversight. Trump's White House characterized the voluntary accord as a "morally binding" compact that would allow industry innovation while companies police themselves.

The action is Newsom's last major policy push before he terms out of office in January, and it arrives weeks before midterm elections that will determine control of Congress. Newsom, who has been openly positioning for a possible 2028 presidential run, used the occasion to warn that "there will not be a free and fair election in 2028" unless Democrats retake the House in November.

stories.headline: Prominent Zimbabwean Tycoon Wicknell Chivayo Killed in Helicopter Crash
stories.summary:
Zimbabwean businessman Wicknell Chivayo, one of the country's most high-profile and controversial figures, was killed along with his wife Lucy Muteke and four others when their helicopter crashed in the Marondera rural area approximately 70 kilometers east of Harare on Wednesday evening. Police confirmed all six people aboard the aircraft died; two of the six were pilots. The helicopter went down roughly 40 minutes after takeoff from a rural property Chivayo was developing.

Chivayo, widely known as "Sir Wicknell," built a public profile through government contracts, philanthropy, and conspicuous displays of wealth on social media, including gifting luxury cars and large sums of money to musicians and religious leaders. His business dealings repeatedly attracted scrutiny, most notably a $172 million solar power project in Gwanda awarded to his company Intratrek Zimbabwe, which became the subject of years of legal disputes. Zimbabwe's anti-corruption commission investigated him over election-related procurement contracts but closed the inquiry in 2025, saying it found no evidence of wrongdoing.

The cause of the crash was not immediately known, and police said investigations were under way. Kenya's President William Ruto, who had appeared publicly with Chivayo, paid tribute to him following news of his death. The crash removes one of the most politically connected and polarizing private figures in southern African business circles.
